question.text:
A homomorphism from a group of order 72 has an image of order 12. How many elements map
to a fixed element of its image?
(A) 3 (B) 6 (C) 12 (D) 24 (E) 60

solution.text:
The kernel has order 72/12 = 6. Each nonempty fiber is a coset of the kernel, so every spec-
ified image element has exactly six preimages.

question.text:
Let f : Z → Z be defined by f(x) = 10x. What is | ker f |?
36 24
(A) 2 (B) 3 (C) 6 (D) 9 (E) 12

solution.text:
The map is well defined since 24 | 10 · 36. The kernel condition is 24 | 10x, equivalent to
12 | x. In Z the possibilities are 0, 12, 24, so the kernel has order three.

question.text:
Let G have prime order p, and let f : G → H be a homomorphism whose image contains an
element other than the identity. Which must be true?
(A) f is onto H. (B) H has order p.
(C) f is injective. (D) H is Abelian.
(E) f(g) = g for every g ∈ G.

solution.text:
The kernel is a subgroup of a prime-order group, so its order is either 1 or p. The latter
would make the entire image the identity, contrary to the hypothesis. Thus the kernel is
trivial and f is injective. Its codomain can be larger and non-Abelian.

solution.text:
Kernels are normal. Conjugating (12) by (123) gives (23), which is outside {e, (12)}. The
other three occur as kernels of the identity map, the sign map, and the trivial map, respec-
tively.

question.text:
For an integer m > 1, define f : (Z, +) → (mZ, +) by f (k) = mk. Which statement is correct?
(A) f is not a homomorphism because m ̸= 1.
(B) f is injective but not surjective.
(C) f is surjective but not injective.
(D) f is an isomorphism onto a proper subgroup of Z.
(E) f is an automorphism of Z.

solution.text:
The stated codomain is mZ: every element there is mk for a unique integer k. Addition is
preserved, so f is an isomorphism. Yet mZ is a proper subgroup of Z. This can happen
for infinite groups; a finite group cannot be isomorphic to a proper subgroup because
cardinalities would differ.
